The primary's mean validation R@10 is 0.0335. That is about 6x chance (≈0.0054) and beats CCA in all 4 folds (0.0179; +0.016 ± 0.009). So the alignment is real but weak, which is expected when held-out patients contain many spots that look nearly identical. For prediction from histology the primary is tied with ridge (Pearson top-50: 0.148 vs 0.152; better in 2/4 folds). For clustering it is tied with the unimodal and CCA baselines. However, the hard_infonce comparison beats the primary on R@10 in every fold (0.0539/0.0211/0.0347/0.0510 vs 0.0492/0.0148/0.0319/0.0382). Its mean is 0.040 vs 0.034, with paired differences of +0.0028 to +0.0128 (mean +0.0066, SD ≈0.0044). The automated flag calls the hard_infonce gap 'within noise', but the paired, per-fold comparison is consistent. Every fold improves: a paired t of about 3.0 with 3 degrees of freedom, and a sign test of 4/4. That is moderate evidence, not conclusive. There is also a plausible reason for the gain. Soft InfoNCE spreads target probability across spots with similar expression (23% are near-twins). That rewards retrieving look-alikes instead of the exact paired spot, and exact pairing is what R@10 measures. Hard InfoNCE also leaves the regression term and every other setting unchanged, so it should not cost anything on prediction. Its training curves overfit faster: train loss falls to about 2.0 while validation loss stays around 8–9, and folds 2 and 3 peak early (epochs 7 and 3). Early stopping on the retrieval score already handles this, and the selected checkpoints still beat the primary's. Switching needs no extra compute and carries no risk of a regression.
